dervis-irab:1-14.t:
* Vocabulary:
(كُوِّرَتْ) it was wrapped up and its light taken away. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "كار الرجل العمامة كورا, of the pattern قال: he wound the turban around his head. Every turn is a كور, named by the maṣdar (verbal noun); its plural is أكوار, like ثوب and أثواب. كوّرها, with doubling, is intensive; and from it one says كورت الشيء when you wrap it in a circular manner. The saying of the Exalted إذا الشمس كوّرت means: it was rolled up like the rolling up of a scroll." Al-Zamakhsharī's wording: "There are two views on التكوير. It may be from كورت العمامة when you wind it, i.e. its light is wrapped up so that its spreading and diffusion over the horizons goes away; this is an expression for removing it and taking it away, because as long as it remains, its light is spread out and not wrapped up. Or its wrapping may be an expression for lifting it up and covering it, because when a garment is to be put away it is wrapped and folded; similar to it is His saying: يوم نطوي السماء. Or it may be from طعنه فجوّره وكوّره, when he throws him down, i.e. it is thrown and cast down from its orbit, just as the stars were described with الانكدار." What the lexicons have set out can be summarized as follows: "كار يكور كورا العمامة على رأسه: he wound it and wrapped it around; كور الله الليل على النهار: He made this enter into that; كورت الشمس: its light was gathered and wrapped as the turban is wrapped; it has been said: it faded away and departed."
(انْكَدَرَتْ) they fell and dropped onto the earth. The basic sense of الانكدار is pouring down. Abū ʿUbayda said: انكدرت means they swooped down, as the eagle swoops down when it folds its wings. Al-ʿAjjāj said, describing a falcon:
أبصر حرمات فلاة فانكدر ... تقصي البازي إذا البازي كسر
(He caught sight of the forbidden creatures of a desert and swooped down, as the hawk swoops when the hawk folds its wings.)
(الْعِشارُ) pregnant she-camels, the plural of عشراء, like نفاس as the plural of نفساء. She is the one whose pregnancy has reached ten months; that then remains her name until she gives birth at the completion of the year, and she is the most precious thing her owners have. It is narrated that the Prophet ﷺ passed among his Companions by some pregnant she-camels and lowered his gaze. It was said to him: "These are the most precious of our wealth; why do you not look at them?" He said: "Allah has forbidden me that," then recited: ولا تمدنّ عينيك (the verse).
(سُجِّرَتْ) سجر يسجر سجرا, of the pattern نصر, التنور: he filled the oven with fuel and heated it; سجر الماء النهر: the water filled the river; سجر البحر: the sea overflowed; سجر الماء في حلقه: he poured it; سجر الكلب: he tied the dog with the ساجور (collar); سجر الشيء: he let it loose. This is what the lexicons have mentioned regarding this root. In al-Asās: "كلب مسجور, مسجّر and مسوجر; I سجرته, سجّرته and سوجرته: I put the ساجور on him, which is an iron collar studded with nails with sharp points. بحر مسجور and مسجّر, and عين مسجورة and مسجّرة: brim-full. سجر السيل الآبار والأحساء (the torrent filled the wells and the water-pits); 'We passed by every حاجر and ساجر', which is every place a torrent has passed and filled. سجر التنور: he filled it with سجور, which is its fuel; and he سجره with the مسجرة, which is the poker. Of the figurative usages: سجرت الناقة سجرا and سجّرت تسجيرا: the she-camel drew out her yearning cry after her young one and filled her mouth with it. He said:
حنّت إلى برك فقلت لها: قرّي ... بعض الحنين فإن سجرك شائقي
(She yearned for a herd of camels, and I said to her: hold back some of your yearning, for your yearning cry stirs my longing.)
And from it: ساجرته مساجرة, which is close friendship and intermixing; he is my سجير and they are my سجراء, because each of the two yearns for the other. And from it: ماء أسجر, water mixed with turbidity and redness from rainwater; one says: 'There is سجرة in it', 'it is أسجر', 'a قطرة سجراء (reddish drop)', and 'عين سجراء'. Al-Ḥuwaydira said:
بغريض سارية أدرّته الصبا ... من ماء أسجر أطيب المستنقع
(With fresh water of a night-cloud which the east wind made flow, from reddish water, the sweetest of pools.)
عين سجراء: [an eye] whose white is mixed with redness; 'There is سجرة in your eye'; and 'on their necks are السواجير', i.e. the fetters." Something of the meaning of this root has already passed in al-Ṭūr. Accordingly, the views on what is meant by it here are many. Al-Qurṭubī, as is his habit, counted the views on it, and we point to them briefly:
1- وإذا البحار سجرت: i.e. they were filled with water, so that some of them overflow into others and they become one thing.
2- It has been said: their fresh water was let loose upon their salt water until they were filled.
3- It has been said: they became one sea.
4- It has been said: they dried up, so that not one drop of their water remains.
5- It has been said: they were set alight and became fire.
6- It has been said: it is the redness of their water, until it becomes as though it were blood.
(الْمَوْؤُدَةُ) He said in al-Asās: "وأد ابنته: he weighed her down with earth. «وإذا الموءودة سئلت». Al-Farazdaq said:
وجدي الذي منع الوائدات ... وأحيا الوئيد فلم يوأد
(And my grandfather is the one who stopped the women who buried girls alive, and gave life to the buried girl, so that she was not buried.)"
وأد ابنته يئدها, of the pattern ضرب: he buried her in the earth while she was alive; so the daughter is وئيد, وئيدة and موءودة. Al-Zamakhsharī said in al-Kashshāf: "وأد يئد is a metathesis (maqlūb) of آد يئود, when it weighs down. Allah the Exalted said: ولا يئوده حفظهما. [It is so called] because it is weighing down with earth." Abū Ḥayyān followed this up in al-Baḥr and said: "It cannot be claimed of وأد that it is a metathesis of آد, because each of the two is fully conjugated in the past, the imperative, the imperfect, the maṣdar, the active participle and the passive participle, and there is nothing in it of the grounds that justify claiming metathesis. What tells originality apart from metathesis is that one of the two arrangements has a rule that testifies to its originality while the other does not; or that it is free of augment letters while the other has an augment; or that it is more fully conjugated while the other is not; or that it is more frequently used than the other — this being as established and settled in the science of morphology. The first is like يئس and أيس, the second like طأمن and اطمأن, the third like شوائع and شواع, and the fourth like لعمري and رعملي."

* I'rab:
(إِذَا الشَّمْسُ كُوِّرَتْ) (إذا) is a future adverb containing the meaning of condition; its apodosis (jawāb al-sharṭ), in the twelve places where it occurs, is His saying (علمت نفس), as will come, and it is attached (mutaʿalliq) to its apodosis. (الشمس) is the nāʾib fāʿil (deputy agent) of an implied verb explained by what follows. Al-Zamakhsharī inclined to this and disallowed its being nominative as a mubtadaʾ (subject), because إذا calls for a verb on account of the meaning of condition in it; but what al-Zamakhsharī disallowed — a mubtadaʾ occurring after it — the Kufans and al-Akhfash among the Basrans permitted. The clause (كورت) is explicative and has no grammatical position.
(وَإِذَا النُّجُومُ انْكَدَرَتْ) conjoined to what preceded and parsed like it; but (النجوم) here is the fāʿil (agent) of a verb explained by His saying (انكدرت).
(وَإِذَا الْجِبالُ سُيِّرَتْ، وَإِذَا الْعِشارُ عُطِّلَتْ) also conjoined. (الجبال) and (العشار) are the deputy agents of an omitted verb. The meaning of their being left idle is their being left without a herdsman and without milking, on account of the calamity that has befallen them.
(وَإِذَا الْوُحُوشُ حُشِرَتْ) also conjoined.
(وَإِذَا الْبِحارُ سُجِّرَتْ وَإِذَا النُّفُوسُ زُوِّجَتْ) also conjoined. The meaning is: the spirits were returned to their bodies; this is based on التزويج meaning making a thing a pair, with النفوس on this view meaning the spirits. It has also been said: every person is coupled with his party and every like with its like, so the righteous man is coupled with the righteous man in Paradise.
(وَإِذَا الْمَوْؤُدَةُ سُئِلَتْ بِأَيِّ ذَنْبٍ قُتِلَتْ) also conjoined. (بأي) is a preposition and its genitive noun attached to (قتلت), and the clause stands in place of the second object of (سئلت). When a daughter was born to one of the Arabs and he let her live, he would dress her in a garment of wool or hair and leave her to herd the camels and sheep. If he wanted to kill her, he would leave her until, when she was six years old, he would say to her mother: "Perfume her and adorn her, so that I may take her to her in-laws." He would have dug a pit or a well in the desert; he would take her to it and say to her: "Look into it," then push her from behind and heap earth upon her until the well was level with the ground. Al-Farazdaq — Abū Firās Hammām ibn Ghālib ibn Ṣaʿṣaʿa — boasted of his grandfather Ṣaʿṣaʿa, since he had prevented the burying alive of daughters, as has preceded.
(وَإِذَا الصُّحُفُ نُشِرَتْ وَإِذَا السَّماءُ كُشِطَتْ وَإِذَا الْجَحِيمُ سُعِّرَتْ وَإِذَا الْجَنَّةُ أُزْلِفَتْ) also conjoined to what preceded.
(عَلِمَتْ نَفْسٌ ما أَحْضَرَتْ) The clause has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of (إذا), as has preceded. (علمت نفس) is a past verb and its fāʿil, (ما) is a mafʿūl bihi (direct object), and the clause (أحضرت) has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila (relative clause) of (ما).

* Rhetoric:
Indefiniteness (al-tankīr):
In His saying «علمت نفس ما أحضرت» there is indefiniteness in (نفس), and its benefit is generality. An objector may object that an indefinite noun conveys generality only when it is in the context of negation; accordingly, here it occurs in the context of affirmation, where it is for singularity or for kind — so how can singularity or kind agree with a setting suited to generality? The answer to this objection is that what was mentioned about its being in the context of negation and affirmation is a general tendency, not a universal rule, so it does not preclude generality sometimes being intended by it with the help of the setting. There is another answer to this objection: the indefinite noun here occurs in the context of a condition, and the context of a condition is like [that of negation] [Translator's note: the source has كسياق النكرة, apparently for كسياق النفي] in that the indefinite noun is for generality when it occurs in either of them.

dervis-irab:15-29.t:
* Vocabulary:
(بِالْخُنَّسِ) الخنس: all the stars, or only the planets among them, or some of them; from الخنس, which is going back, because they go back in their course behind them. The verb is خنس يخنس, of the pattern دخل. In al-Ṣiḥāḥ: "الخنس are all the stars, because they recede (تخنس) at setting and because they are hidden by day; and it is said: they are the planets among them, to the exclusion of the fixed stars." Al-Farrāʾ said on the saying of the Exalted فلا أقسم بالخنس الجواري الكنس that they are the five stars: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, Venus and Mercury, because they recede in their course and withdraw (تكنس) as gazelles withdraw into their lairs. الخنس is also the shelter of gazelles, and the gazelles themselves, and wild cows.
(الْكُنَّسِ) In al-Miṣbāḥ: "كناس الظبي, with kasra, is the gazelle's dwelling; كنس الظبي كنوسا, of the pattern نزل: it entered its lair; تكنس الظبي: it went out of sight and hid in its lair; تكنس الرجل: he entered the tent; تكنست المرأة: she entered the litter (al-hawdaj)."
(عَسْعَسَ) it advanced with its darkness, or retreated. Al-ʿAjjāj said:
حتى إذا الصبح لها تنفسا ... وانجاب عنها ليلها وعسعسا
(Until, when the morning breathed for her, and her night was rent away from her and departed.)

* I'rab:
(فَلا أُقْسِمُ بِالْخُنَّسِ، الْجَوارِ الْكُنَّسِ، وَاللَّيْلِ إِذا عَسْعَسَ، وَالصُّبْحِ إِذا تَنَفَّسَ) The fāʾ is resumptive. The discussion of (لا) has preceded, so refresh your memory of it. (أقسم) is an imperfect verb in the nominative (marfūʿ), its fāʿil (agent) latent (mustatir), its implied form being "anā". (بالخنس) is attached (mutaʿalliq) to (أقسم). (الجواري) is a naʿt (adjective) or badal (substitute), and (الكنس) is a naʿt of (الجواري). (والليل): the wāw is also for the oath; (الليل) is genitive (majrūr) by the wāw of oath, and the preposition and its genitive noun are attached to an omitted verb, its implied form being "أقسم". (إذا) is an adverb attached to the verb of oath, and the clause (عسعس) is in the position of the genitive by the adverb's annexation to it. (والصبح إذا تنفس) is conjoined to the preceding clause. We did not conjoin (الليل) to (الخنس) only because the wāw is the beginning of [a new] oath.
If it is said: "Then you have contradicted Sībawayh, for he does not regard the wāw that follows an oath as the beginning of an oath, but as a conjunction; and you have made the first wāw, which follows an oath, the beginning of an oath?" We say: Sībawayh spoke only about the wāw [of oath]; as for the verse, the first oath in it is with the bāʾ and the verb, so we made the wāw after that an oath and a follower; and that is more eloquent, as though He swore by two different things.
If it is said: "Indeed, Sībawayh spoke only about the wāw that follows an oath; so what is the difference between a wāw that follows an oath made with the wāw and a wāw that follows an oath made with the bāʾ, when they are nothing but the same? For each of them is an instrument for it, and the tāʾ indicates the bāʾ, so their rule is one." We say: they are not the same. When the oath begins with the wāw and is followed by another wāw, making the other an oath involves a distasteful repetition, since the instrument is one. That is not so in the verse, since the instrument differs, so the [distasteful] effect of repetition is then avoided. Do you not see that if the oath began with the wāw and was then followed by an oath with the bāʾ, it would be necessary to make them two independent oaths? So likewise if this order were reversed. Moreover, if what prevented Sībawayh from making the second wāw an independent oath was that the apodosis comes as a single one and that the first wāw would need something omitted, while conjunction makes the assumption of an omitted element unnecessary — then this does not necessarily extend to the bāʾ, because it is the root of the oath, especially with the verb of oath stated explicitly and then emphasized by the addition of (لا); for in all of that together there is what makes it unnecessary to give it its own stated apodosis. That is not so with the wāw, for its standing in the oath is weak in comparison with the bāʾ. So it does not follow from the omission of an apodosis whose indication is firmly established that an apodosis less clear than it may be omitted.
We close the discussion of this question with an excellent subtle point: I restricted the raising of the question to the second wāw, in His saying (والليل إذا عسعس), and not the third, because it does not apply to it. Do you not see that if you made it a conjunction you would not be committed to conjoining onto two governors, because you would make it stand in for the bāʾ and make (إذا) in it accusative directly by the verb, since no adverb preceded in the verb's clause onto which (إذا) could be conjoined? It then becomes like your saying مررت بزيد وعمرو اليوم (I passed by Zayd and ʿAmr today): (اليوم) is accusative directly by the verb, and it is understood from the example that your passing by Zayd is unrestricted, not qualified by an adverb, and that only your passing by ʿAmr in particular is qualified by (اليوم). But [does this] match the verse? For the adverb in it, even though the verb governs it directly, qualifies the oath by the night, not the oath by الخنس.
(إِنَّهُ لَقَوْلُ رَسُولٍ كَرِيمٍ) The clause has no grammatical position because it is the apodosis of the oath. (إنّ) and its noun; the lām is the shifted lām (al-lām al-muzaḥlaqa); (قول) is its khabar (predicate), (رسول) is muḍāf ilayhi, and (كريم) is a naʿt. What is meant by it will come in the section on Benefits.
(ذِي قُوَّةٍ عِنْدَ ذِي الْعَرْشِ مَكِينٍ مُطاعٍ ثَمَّ أَمِينٍ) (ذي قوة) is a second adjective of (رسول). (عند ذي العرش) is a ḥāl (circumstantial) of (مسكين) [Translator's note: so in the source; read مكين], because it was originally an adjective of it, and when it was placed first it became accusative as a ḥāl. (مكين) is a third adjective and (مطاع) a fourth adjective. (ثم) is an adverb meaning "there", attached to (مطاع). (أمين) is a fifth adjective.
(وَما صاحِبُكُمْ بِمَجْنُونٍ) The wāw is a conjunction, and the clause is conjoined to (إنه لقول رسول كريم). (ما) is the Ḥijāzī negative ما, (صاحبكم) is its noun, the bāʾ is a redundant (zāʾida) preposition, and (مجنون) is genitive in form, accusative in position, as the khabar of (ما).
(وَلَقَدْ رَآهُ بِالْأُفُقِ الْمُبِينِ) conjoined to His saying (إنه لقول …), so it falls within the scope of what is sworn. The lām is the answer to an omitted oath, (قد) is a particle of realization, (رآه) is a past verb with a latent fāʿil [and its object], (بالأفق) is attached to (رآه), and (المبين) is a naʿt of (الأفق).
(وَما هُوَ عَلَى الْغَيْبِ بِضَنِينٍ) also conjoined. (ما) is the Ḥijāzī negative ما and (هو) its noun; (على الغيب) is attached to (ضنين); the bāʾ is a redundant preposition, and (ضنين) is genitive in form, accusative in position, as the khabar of (ما). (على) means the bāʾ, i.e. he does not withhold it from you but informs you of it. It was also read بظنين, with the dotted ẓāʾ, i.e. suspected. In al-Miṣbāḥ: "الظنة, with kasra, is suspicion; it is a noun from ظننته, of the pattern قتل, when you suspected him; so he is ظنين, a faʿīl in the sense of a passive participle (mafʿūl). Among the Seven [readings]: وما هو على الغيب بظنين, i.e. suspected." Also in al-Miṣbāḥ: "ضن بالشيء يضنّ, of the pattern تعب, ضنا and ضنّة with kasra and ضنانة with fatḥa: he was miserly, so he is miserly; and the pattern ضرب is a dialectal variant of it."
(وَما هُوَ بِقَوْلِ شَيْطانٍ رَجِيمٍ) also conjoined; it is a negation of their saying that it is soothsaying and sorcery.
(فَأَيْنَ تَذْهَبُونَ) The fāʾ is a conjunction. (أين) is an interrogative noun in the position of the accusative as an adverb of place, vague rather than specific, attached to (تذهبون). (تذهبون) is an imperfect verb in the nominative and its fāʿil; i.e. which road are you taking?
(إِنْ هُوَ إِلَّا ذِكْرٌ لِلْعالَمِينَ لِمَنْ شاءَ مِنْكُمْ أَنْ يَسْتَقِيمَ) (إن) is negative, (هو) is a mubtadaʾ (subject), (إلا) is a particle of restriction, and (ذكر) is the khabar. (للعالمين) is attached to (ذكر) or is a naʿt of it. (لمن) is a badal from His saying (للعالمين), with repetition of the governor, which is the lām. The clause (شاء) has no grammatical position because it is the ṣila (relative clause) of (من); (منكم) is a ḥāl; and (أن) with what is in its scope is the mafʿūl bihi (direct object) of (شاء).
(وَما تَشاؤُنَ إِلَّا أَنْ يَشاءَ اللَّهُ رَبُّ الْعالَمِينَ) The wāw is a conjunction, (ما) is negative, (تشاءون) is an imperfect verb in the nominative and the wāw is its fāʿil, and (إلا) is a particle of restriction. (أن) and what follows it are in the position of the accusative by removal of the preposition, and the [implied] preposition and its genitive noun are attached to (تشاءون). (الله) is the fāʿil, and (رب العالمين) is a badal or naʿt of (الله). Al-Bayḍāwī preferred making the interpreted maṣdar accusative as an adverb (ẓarfiyya); his wording: "And you do not will uprightness, O you who will it, except that Allah wills — i.e. except at the time that Allah wills your willing; so to Him belongs the favour, and the right is upon you for your uprightness."

* Benefits:
The exegetes differed. A great multitude of them held that what is meant by the noble messenger here, down to the last of the attributes, is Muḥammad ﷺ; if the matter is so, that is Allah's customary favour upon His Prophet. A great multitude of them also held that what is meant by it is Jibrīl, upon him be peace. Disagreement has arisen over the relative merit of the angels and the messengers. The well-known position of Abū al-Ḥasan al-Ashʿarī is to prefer the messengers, and the doctrine of the Muʿtazila is to prefer the angels. However, those who differed agreed that it is not permissible to prefer either of the two exalted groups in a way that implies disparaging a specific one of the angels or a specific one of the messengers, because even though preference is established, specifying [the one surpassed] is hurtful to the one surpassed. On this the skilled scholars interpreted his saying ﷺ: "Do not prefer me over Yūnus ibn Mattā," i.e. do not specify one surpassed in particular; for preference in general is established by the consensus of the Muslims, i.e. the preference of the Prophet ﷺ over all the prophets together. Ibn Fāris, may Allah have mercy on him, used to clarify this with an example, saying: if you said in the presence of a group of jurists, "So-and-so is the best of the people of his age," the group would bear this preference, even though it entails their inclusion among those surpassed; but if you specified one of them and said, "So-and-so is better than you," the hurt would quickly reach some of you.
Al-Qāḍī al-Bayḍāwī said: "It has been used as evidence for the superiority of Jibrīl over Muḥammad, upon both of them be blessing and peace, since He enumerated the excellences of Jibrīl and limited Himself to denying madness of him ﷺ. That is weak, since what is intended by it is to refute their saying 'it is only a human being who teaches him' and 'has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there madness in him?', not to enumerate their merits and weigh them against each other."
As for al-Karkhī, he said: "Then, if you look closely, you will realize that applying those attributes to Jibrīl in this setting is an insertion (idmāj) of the glorification of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and that he reached such standing and loftiness of rank with the Lord of the Throne that the envoy between Him and him was made one like this angel, brought near, obeyed and trustworthy. So the statement of these attributes, with respect to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, is an elevation of rank for him, just like the statement 'with the Lord of the Throne' with respect to the elevation of the rank of Jibrīl, upon him be peace."
As for al-Zamakhsharī, he produced something which perhaps Jibrīl, Allah's blessings be upon him, would not have been pleased with, a shortcoming in the right of the bearer of good news and the warner, by saying: "This suffices you as evidence of the standing of Jibrīl, upon him be peace, and his superiority over the angels, and of the difference from the rank of the best of humans, Muḥammad ﷺ, if you weigh the two mentions when He paired them, and compare His saying: إنه لقول رسول كريم، ذي قوة عند ذي العرش مكين، مطاع ثم أمين with His saying: وما صاحبكم بمجنون."
Ibn al-Munayyir, as is his habit, refuted al-Zamakhsharī, saying: "Then the discussion returns to the verse, after granting that Jibrīl is meant and after we entrust to Allah [the reckoning for] his specifying the Prophet ﷺ and counting him the one surpassed. We say: no attribute is mentioned in it but the Prophet ﷺ has its like. The first of them is رسول كريم; He said with respect to him ﷺ at the end of Sūrat al-Ḥāqqa: إنه لقول رسول كريم. It has also been said that Jibrīl is meant there, but His saying وما هو بقول شاعر rejects that, and al-Zamakhsharī agreed with that earlier. So this is the first of the attributes [Translator's note: the source has الفوت, apparently for النعوت] and the greatest of them. As for His saying ذي قوة, it is not the point of dispute, since there is no contention that Jibrīl, upon him be peace, has superiority in bodily strength; whoever uproots cities with a feather of his wing — there is no disputing the superiority of his strength over the strength of humans; this has been said in explaining His saying ذو مرة فاستوى. As for His saying عند ذي العرش مكين مطاع ثم أمين, the obedience of the angels has also been established [Translator's note: the source prints نبتت for ثبتت] for our Prophet ﷺ. It has come that Jibrīl, upon him be peace, said to the Prophet: 'Allah conveys greetings of peace to you, and He has ordered the angel of the mountains to obey you,' when Quraysh harmed him; so the angel greeted him and said: 'If you order me to bring the two mountains (al-Akhshabān) together upon them, I will do it'; but the Prophet ﷺ was patient and sought the reward. The greatest and noblest of that is his Praised Station in the Great Intercession, on the day when no one goes before him, when Allah the Exalted will say to him: 'Raise your head; speak and you will be heard; ask and you will be given; intercede and your intercession will be accepted.' As for أمين, he said: 'By Allah, I am trustworthy on earth and trustworthy in heaven.' And sufficient for you is His saying وما هو على الغيب بظنين: if you read it with the ẓāʾ, its meaning is that he ﷺ is trustworthy over the unseen and not suspected; and if you read it with the ḍād, it goes back to generosity. So how can one argue for preference by means of attributes shared equally by the superior and the surpassed?"

* Rhetoric:
1- In His saying «والليل إذا عسعس والصبح إذا تنفس» there is an implicit metaphor (istiʿāra makniyya). He likened the night to a person who advances and retreats, then omitted the thing compared to [Translator's note: the source says المشبه (the thing compared), though in an implicit metaphor it is the المشبه به that is omitted] and took one of its attributes, namely the word عسعس, i.e. it advanced and retreated. Likewise He likened the morning to a living being that breathes, omitted [the thing compared to], and brought one of its attributes, namely breathing, i.e. the exit of breath from the interior. Or it may be said that He likened the night to a distressed, grieving person who is confined so that he does not move; when he breathes, he finds his relief. Here, when the morning rises, it is as though it has been entirely freed from grief, so that was expressed by breathing.
2- In His saying «فلا أقسم بالخنس الجوار الكنس» there is the device of al-iltizām (self-imposed constraint), for the nūn is kept before the sīn.
